newsitem.title: UK: POLL-British budget finds favour with voters.
newsitem.headline: POLL-British budget finds favour with voters.

text.p: The British Labour party's first budget since coming to power in May has won the approval of the nation, even though most people reckon on being worse off, a national opinion poll showed.

The poll showed 54 percent of those surveyed thought Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown had done a good job with Wednesday's "people's budget", which he said had been necessary for the long-term health of the economy.
Only 13 percent thought Brown had done a bad job, according to the telephone survey of 505 adults, which was conducted by NOP on behalf of the Political Context public affairs constancy.

A clear majority said they thought the budget was fair for the whole country, but a rise in duties on cigarettes, petrol and alcohol and a cut in tax relief for home owners left most people believing they would be out of pocket.
Some 47 percent thought they would personally be worse off after the budget, while 45 percent believed it would make no difference, the poll showed.

Asked to apportion blame for the tax rises contained in the budget, 53 percent of the sample said the measures had been necessary because the former Conservative government had left the economy in a bad shape.
Just less than one in five thought the tax rises were the fault of the Labour party.
